summary: Specifies how to map the Real-time Transport Protocol onto the Datagram Congestion Control Protocol, along with how to signal it with SDP. DCCP offers congestion control for real-time applications. It is on the standards track.

eli5.summary: RTP is a way to send live sound and video, and DCCP is a road that slows traffic politely when it is crowded. This document says how to put one on the other.

questions: how to run rtp over dccp
what port does rtp over dccp use
how to signal dccp in sdp
subtitle: How to carry real-time audio and video (RTP) over DCCP so it gets congestion control without extra work in the application.

tldr.problem: Many real-time RTP applications do not implement congestion control, which risks congestion collapse, and building it into each application is hard.
tldr.mechanism: Each RTP or RTCP packet rides in one DCCP datagram, and new SDP values and service codes announce that a media session runs over DCCP.
tldr.outcome: Applications get a choice of congestion control from the transport. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and was later updated by RFC 6773.

facts.label: Packing rule
facts.value: One RTP packet per DCCP datagram

today: RFC 5762 is a Proposed Standard published in April 2010. It has been updated by RFC 6773 and has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Why Run RTP over DCCP
sections.content:
RTP is widely used for video streaming and telephony, but many real-time applications do not implement congestion control. That creates the potential for congestion collapse of the network. RFC 3551 already says that RTP receivers SHOULD monitor packet loss and keep it within acceptable parameters.

The RFC describes two ways to get congestion control. One is to extend RTP itself, for example to allow TCP Friendly Rate Control at the application level. That passes the complexity to application authors. The other is to run RTP over a transport that already has congestion control. TCP is a poor fit for most interactive real-time uses because it is reliable and its congestion control reacts in ways that do not suit them. SCTP is inappropriate for similar reasons.

DCCP offers unreliable packet delivery and a choice of congestion control, and it leaves the implementation work to the operating system. The RFC says that if DCCP becomes widely available, these are expected to be compelling advantages.
sections.eli5: If everyone sends video as fast as they like, the network jams. DCCP is a traffic cop built into the road, so each app does not need its own.

sections.title: Framing RTP Data Packets
sections.content:
Each RTP data packet MUST be carried in a single DCCP datagram. The RTP header is read exactly as the RTP specification says. The RTP sequence number and the DCCP sequence number have different meanings, so one cannot be worked out from the other.

A DCCP connection is opened when an end system joins an RTP session and stays open for the whole session. To keep NAT bindings alive, an end system SHOULD send a zero-length DCCP-Data packet once every 15 seconds when it has nothing else to send. This is not needed if the DCCP CCID already provides a transport-level keepalive, or if there is no NAT on the path.

RTP data MUST obey DCCP congestion control. If the allowed rate falls below what the payload format would use, the application can use a rate-adaptive payload format or switch among several formats. RTP extensions that add their own application-level congestion control conflict with DCCP and MUST NOT be used.

DCCP can use partial checksums, so packets with corrupt payloads may still be delivered. An RTP end system MAY enable this when the payload format has mechanisms to cope with corruption. The checksum MUST then cover at least the DCCP and RTP headers, and partial checksums MUST NOT be used unless the payload format supports them.
sections.eli5: Each little piece of the video goes in its own envelope. If the network is busy, the sender has to send fewer envelopes, so the app should be ready to send a lower-quality picture.

sections.title: RTCP, Multiplexing and Sessions
sections.content:
RTCP, the control side of RTP, is used in the standard way. Each compound RTCP packet travels in a single DCCP datagram. RTCP packets MUST also obey DCCP congestion control, so a report can be delayed when capacity is short. The time it is actually sent is used to compute the next RTCP transmission time. If the DCCP connection can carry much less than the nominal session bandwidth, participants may time out, so session parameters SHOULD be renegotiated, for example with a re-invite and an updated b= line in SIP.

RTCP reports and DCCP acknowledgement options can overlap, most clearly the Loss RLE Report Blocks of RTCP Extended Reports and the DCCP Ack Vector option. If they overlap, an application SHOULD use one or the other, not both.

The obvious mapping uses two DCCP connections per RTP flow, one for data and one for control. To save ports and ease NAT traversal, the RFC RECOMMENDS multiplexing RTP and RTCP on a single DCCP connection following RFC 5761, where possible.

An end system SHOULD NOT assume it will see only one synchronisation source (SSRC), since an RTP session can span several connections and include mixers or translators. A translator that joins several DCCP connections must track the congestion state of each and adapt the media to each.
sections.eli5: The sender also sends little progress reports. They share the same road rules, and they can ride in the same lane as the video to save space.

sections.title: Which RTP Profiles Work
sections.content:
Most RTP profiles can be used over DCCP. There are two exceptions. A profile that cannot tolerate packet corruption may conflict with DCCP partial checksums, for example the integrity protection of RTP/SAVP. A profile that requires a particular non-DCCP lower-layer transport also conflicts. Profiles in these cases SHOULD NOT be used with DCCP unless the conflicting features can be disabled.

Four profiles MAY be used with DCCP: the minimal-control audio and video profile (RFC 3551), SRTP (RFC 3711), the feedback profile (RFC 4585) and the secure feedback profile (RFC 5124).
sections.eli5: Almost every kind of RTP can ride on DCCP. The few that cannot are the ones that insist on a different road.

sections.title: Signalling with SDP
sections.content:
Sessions are described with the Session Description Protocol (SDP) in an m= line. This RFC defines five values for the proto field: DCCP, DCCP/RTP/AVP, DCCP/RTP/SAVP, DCCP/RTP/AVPF and DCCP/RTP/SAVPF. The plain DCCP value MUST NOT be used to signal RTP sessions. RTP payload types use the payload type number as the fmt value, with an rtpmap attribute when the number is dynamic.

DCCP port 5004 is registered for these RTP profiles and SHOULD be the default. If RTCP is on a separate connection, it SHOULD use the next higher port unless a=rtcp: says otherwise.

A new media-level attribute, dccp-service-code, announces the DCCP service code. It can be written in hexadecimal, decimal or ASCII form, and a parser MUST compare the numeric value. Registered codes are RTPA (audio), RTPV (video), RTPT (text), RTPO (other media) and RTCP (a separate RTCP connection). Applications SHOULD use them to ease the job of middleboxes.

The a=setup: attribute says which side starts the DCCP connection, used as in RFC 4145 but for DCCP. The a=connection: attribute decides whether a new connection is needed after a later offer and answer. Multiplexed RTP and RTCP MUST be signalled with a=rtcp-mux.
sections.eli5: Before a call starts, the two sides swap a note saying which road, which door number and what kind of traffic they will use. This RFC invents the words for that note.

sections.title: An Offer and Answer Example
sections.content:
In the RFC's example, an offerer at 192.0.2.47 offers an H.261 video session over DCCP/RTP/AVP on port 5004 with service code SC=x52545056, which is RTPV in hexadecimal. RTP and RTCP are multiplexed with a=rtcp-mux, and the offerer is a=setup:passive.

The answerer at 192.0.2.128 replies with the same service code in text form (SC:RTPV) and a=setup:active. It then opens a DCCP connection to port 5004 on the offerer. Port 5004 carries both RTP and RTCP, and port 5005 is unused.
sections.eli5: One side says "I will wait at door 5004," the other says "OK, I will knock." Then they talk through that one door.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of RTP, the chosen profile and payload format, DCCP and the SDP specifications all apply. The RFC expects effective congestion control to help reduce the denial-of-service potential of RTP flows that ignore the advice to cut their rate under persistent congestion.

The main new conflict is between the Secure RTP profiles and DCCP partial checksums. Message authentication codes fail on any bit error, which partial checksums allow. So partial checksums SHOULD NOT be used with SRTP authentication, and the Secure RTP profiles SHOULD NOT be used with partial checksums.
sections.eli5: A secure lock on the envelope breaks if even one letter is smudged. So you should not use the "smudged is fine" option together with the lock.
